A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system that helps websites load quickly no matter where a visitor is located. Normally, every request for a webpage travels all the way back to a single origin server — the main computer where the website's files are originally stored. If that server is far away, pages load slowly. A CDN solves this by placing copies of the website's content on many smaller servers scattered around the world, called edge locations, because they sit at the "edge" of the network, closer to everyday visitors. When someone requests a page, the CDN checks whether a nearby edge location already has a saved copy. If it does, that's called a cache hit, meaning the content can be delivered instantly from nearby storage without bothering the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that all keep copies of popular books, so people do not need to travel to one central library across the country every time someone wants to read something. Only when a book, or webpage, is missing locally does the request travel further to fetch a copy from the source. Because most requests get answered by nearby edge locations, pages load faster, servers stay less crowded, and the whole experience feels smoother, even during high traffic. This is why streaming services, online stores, and news sites rely on CDNs constantly, often without anyone realizing a whole hidden network is quietly doing the work behind the scenes.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's files | It is the ultimate source of truth for content |
| Edge location | A smaller server placed closer to everyday visitors | It shortens the distance data has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered from a nearby saved copy | It makes pages load faster and reduces strain |
| CDN | A network of edge locations working together | It keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
